We demonstrate the value of these three continuous evaluation frameworks using predictions from sepsis models evaluated on two publicly available datasets.

These frameworks provide users of clinical ML models a more realistic understanding of the model’s utility.
Background Clinical machine learning (ML) models are increasingly used to predict patient risk continuously for future adverse events, such as sepsis.

While these metrics—such as Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) and Area Under the Precision Recall curve ( AUPRC)—are widely accepted, they fail to capture how a model behaves when operating continuously in real-world clinical environments.
Moreover, single time point evaluations primarily assess discriminability, which may not directly reflect a model’s clinical utility.

Methods We propose and implement three novel retrospective evaluation frameworks to continuously assess clinical ML models: zone-based, predictive activity monitoring characteristic curve (AMOC)-based and notification-based.
These frameworks were applied to sepsis prediction models using two publicly available clinical datasets.
Results The three continuous evaluation frameworks reveal multiple dimensions of model performance not captured by conventional metrics.
Results The three continuous evaluation frameworks reveal multiple dimensions of model performance not captured by conventional metrics.
Across both datasets, models with high AUROC demonstrate markedly different performance when continuously evaluated.
By uncovering temporal and behavioral aspects of model performance, these methods enable more informed model selection, deployment, and monitoring in healthcare settings.
ML models are used in various branches of medicine such as radiology, cardiology, intensive care.
ML models are used in various branches of medicine such as radiology, cardiology, intensive care.
In this paper, we focus on clinical ML models which are developed to continuously provide a predicted risk of future events or conditions at the bedside.
Examples include early warning scores [ 1 ], patient deterioration index [ 2 ], risk of hypotension [ 3 ], and sepsis prediction [ 4 ].

However, at time of deployment, these ML models continuously produce a score associated with probability of a future event, and classical metrics (e.g., AUROC ) calculated at a single point ahead of events fail to adequately summarize the performance of these continuous predictions over time.
Continuous performance evaluation frameworks for clinical ML models are essential for assessing model efficacy and utility in dynamic medical environments.

Continuous evaluation metrics for ML models are critical to establish anticipated model behavior and clinical utility, including lead time provided by the ML model, alarming rates (both true alarms and false alarms over time), and prediction patterns over time (e.g., risk score evolution and model performance within X hours vs.

A key challenge in evaluating ML models continuously is the occurrence of event of interest.
In a continuous setting, the ML model produces multiple predictions over a time period which may or may not be followed by an event of interest.
The one-to-one mapping of prediction to event of interest (which are used to produce metrics at a single time point evaluation) are unavailable.
The utility score rewarded correct early predictions while penalizing missed predictions and false alarms.
Lead time was defined as the time between the earliest positive prediction and the event such that > 80% of the predictions are positive.
Lastly, regulatory agencies are increasingly identifying the need for continuous evaluation frameworks and metrics for comprehensive model evaluation.
Hence this work aims to fill this gap by providing clinical model developers tools to evaluate models continuously on retrospective datasets.

Zone-based CEF In the zone-based CEF, we partition a patient unit stay in the hospital into time zones, compute scores per time zone and aggregate scores to get a performance metric.
Partition patient’s unit stay : We first partition a patient’s unit stay into time zones.

The rationale for partitioning a stay into time zones is two-fold: one, zoning makes it possible to capture clinical relevance and domain knowledge e.g., time zones before onset of sepsis are more clinically relevant ; two, by defining time zones, we control the contribution of individual scores (described next) from these time zones to the final score.

We sum the individual scores over the entire patient unit stay to get a cumulative score.

Compute best possible score per patient unit stay : We compute the best possible score for each patient unit stay.
Hence, for a patient unit stay with multiple predictions in zones A, B and C, the best possible score would be the sum of scores corresponding to TPs in zone A, TPs in zone B and TNs in zone C.
We add the scores over the entire patient unit stay to get the best possible score.
We compute the continuous score per patient unit stay as the ratio of the cumulative score (step III) divided by the best possible score (step IV).
A patient receives a score of ‘+1’ if the cumulative score for a patient unit stay matches the best possible score.

Our score assignment is as follows, in time zone A, we assign a score of ‘+1’ to TP, ‘−0.5’ to FN, in zone B, we assign a score of ‘+0.5’ to TP and ‘0’ to FN, in zone C, we assign a score of ‘−0.05’ to FP and ‘+1’ to TN, respectively.

The AMOC curve depicts the tradeoff between the speed of detection and the false alarm rate produced by a detection system.

In detection settings, an AMOC curve demonstrates the tradeoff between the elapsed time between the event onset and detection of event (i.e., time to detection ) and the false alarmrate, both of which are desired to be minimized.
The AMOC curve which originally focused on evaluating detection algorithms [ 16 ], needs to be reframed to evaluate predictive ML models that provide continuous score-based predictions.
Applied to prediction tasks, predictive AMOC curves depict tradeoff between anticipation time (elapsed time between a positive prediction and the event onset) and the false alarm rate.
Applied to prediction tasks, predictive AMOC curves depict tradeoff between anticipation time (elapsed time between a positive prediction and the event onset) and the false alarm rate.
Applied to prediction tasks, predictive AMOC curves depict tradeoff between anticipation time (elapsed time between a positive prediction and the event onset) and the false alarm rate.
In detection setting, the detection time is desired to be minimized whereas in prediction settings, the anticipation time needs to be maximized.

With this modification, predictive AMOC curves can be generated to evaluate and compare ML models that provide continuous predictions, and act as a guide to configure predictive algorithms to produce appropriate alarms in clinical settings.
First, we determine a range and resolution for a set of risk thresholds, Z , to sweep through.
For example, sepsis models that produce probability of sepsis onset, the range and an example resolution would be [0,1] and 0.01, respectively.

Second, we sweep through the set of risk thresholds Z and compute anticipation time, or the earliest time a positive prediction occurred within a pre-specified window W hours prior to the event onset.

Second, we sweep through the set of risk thresholds Z and compute anticipation time, or the earliest time a positive prediction occurred within a pre-specified window W hours prior to the event onset.
A positive prediction is produced whenever r t ( n ) > z , z ∈ Z , where r t ( n ) represents the event risk score of the n th patient stay at time stamp t .
Note that the anticipation time is computed only for cases.

For example, if n th patient stay has sepsis at time t sepsis ( n ) and W = 12 h, the first positive prediction within W = 12 h prior to t sepsis ( n ) is taken as the anticipation time for the sepsis patient stay.
Alternatively, W = ∞, considers the first positive prediction (without temporal window limitations) prior to t sepsis ( n ) as the anticipation time for the n th sepsis patient stay.

For cases that do not have a positive prediction within W hours of event onset, we set the anticipation time to be zero, meaning the prediction model failed to make a positive prediction and hence the time available for clinicians to react is zero.

We compute the false alarm rate by [ 1 ] adding any positive predictions for control stays and positive predictions outside the temporal window W for cases and [ 2 ] dividing this sum by the total number of opportunities available to make a false prediction.

For simplicity, we create predictive AMOC curves assuming that the clinician would respond to the very first threshold crossing.
